common_name: Strawberry Fields Deutzia (Deep Pink Hybrid Deutzia)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Strawberry Fields carries unusually deep, saturated pink flowers compared to the pastel tones of most deutzia hybrids.

directions: Strawberry Fields is a robust Deutzia x hybrida selection valued for its unusually deep, rich pink flowers, a stronger and more saturated color than the pastel pinks typical of most deutzia hybrids, borne in dense clusters along gracefully arching branches in late spring to early summer. Its vigorous, upright-arching habit can reach 5 to 6 feet if left unpruned, though an annual hard cutback right after flowering keeps it to a tidier, more compact mound suited to smaller borders. Plant in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, and pinch young stem tips to encourage denser branching and a fuller bloom display. Like other deutzia, it flowers on the previous year's wood, so prune only immediately after the spring bloom to avoid sacrificing next year's flowers.

common_name: Mont Rose Deutzia (Purple-Pink Award-Winning Hybrid Deutzia)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Mont Rose holds a Royal Horticultural Society Award of Garden Merit and stays more compact than most Deutzia x hybrida selections.

directions: Mont Rose is a Royal Horticultural Society Award of Garden Merit deutzia hybrid prized for dense clusters of purplish-pink, star-shaped flowers tinged white at the edges, opening along the branches from late spring into summer, later in the season than many deutzia relatives. Its compact, upright habit stays noticeably smaller than most Deutzia x hybrida selections, fitting foundation plantings and smaller mixed borders where larger deutzia cultivars would need frequent restraint. Plant in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, and prune immediately after flowering by removing some of the oldest stems at the base to keep the shrub renewed and floriferous. Fully hardy and low-maintenance once established, it needs little care beyond this annual post-bloom tidy-up.

common_name: Crimson and Gold Flowering Quince (Red Quince with Golden Stamens)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in any well-drained soil in full sun to part shade; Crimson and Gold's low, spreading habit stays more compact than the larger flowering quince species types.

directions: Crimson and Gold is a compact flowering quince selection named for its striking bicolor blooms — deep crimson-red petals surrounding a bold cluster of bright golden-yellow stamens, a sharper color contrast than the softer stamens of most red quince cultivars. Flowers open directly on the bare, thorny stems in late winter into early spring, well ahead of the foliage, and small yellow-green fruit follows in fall, usable for jelly and preserves though rarely eaten fresh. Its low, spreading habit stays more compact than the larger species types, suiting foundation plantings, low hedges, and mixed borders where a smaller-scale quince is wanted. Extremely tolerant of poor, clay, sandy, or alkaline soil once established; prune only immediately after flowering, since it blooms on old wood.

common_name: Nicoline Flowering Quince (Bright Scarlet Semi-Double Quince)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in any well-drained soil in full sun to part shade; Nicoline grows in a bushier, more upright form than many of the low-spreading flowering quince cultivars.

directions: Nicoline is a densely branched flowering quince selection covered in vivid scarlet-red, cup-shaped flowers with a bright cluster of yellow stamens at the center, opening directly on the thorny bare stems from late winter into early spring. Its bushier, more upright growth than many of the low-spreading quince cultivars gives it good presence as a specimen or informal flowering hedge, and small, hard, yellow-green fruit follows the bloom in fall, usable for jelly and preserves. Extremely tolerant of poor, clay, sandy, or alkaline soil once established and quite drought-tolerant, it blooms on old wood, so prune only right after flowering to avoid removing the following year's flower buds.

common_name: Tiny Wine Gold Ninebark (Compact Golden-Foliage Ninebark)

planting.note: Plant container plants in spring in well-drained to moist soil in full sun; Tiny Wine Gold pairs the compact scale of the Tiny Wine ninebark series with bright golden foliage color.

directions: Tiny Wine Gold combines the small, refined scale of the Tiny Wine ninebark series with brilliant golden-yellow foliage, a color not available on the larger, purple-leaved ninebark cultivars that otherwise dominate the group. New growth emerges its brightest gold in full sun, mellowing slightly through summer, and clusters of small white-to-pink flowers appear in late spring, followed by reddish seed capsules and the exfoliating bark typical of the genus. Its compact, dense habit fits foundation plantings, perennial borders, and smaller landscapes where full-size ninebark cultivars would quickly outgrow the space. Like other ninebark, it tolerates clay, poor soil, and drought once established, and needs only occasional renewal pruning of the oldest stems at the base to stay full and vigorous.

common_name: Lady in Red Ninebark (Red-Purple Foliage Ninebark with Pale Pink Flowers)

planting.note: Plant container plants in spring in well-drained to moist soil in full sun to partial shade; Lady in Red holds its red-purple foliage color reasonably well even in some shade compared with older dark-leaved ninebark cultivars.

directions: Lady in Red is a mid-sized ninebark bred for consistently rich red-purple foliage that holds its color from spring through fall better in partial shade than many older dark-leaved cultivars, which tend to green out without strong sun. Cup-shaped, pale pink flowers cluster along the branches in early summer, followed by reddish-brown seed capsules that persist into fall, and mature stems develop the peeling, multi-layered bark that gives ninebark its common name. Its upright, slightly arching habit suits a mixed shrub border or informal hedge where a taller dark-foliage accent is wanted. Extremely tolerant of clay, poor soil, and periodic flooding once established, it needs only occasional renewal pruning of the oldest stems at the base to stay full and vigorous.

common_name: Aureus Golden Mock Orange (Golden-Foliage Sweet Mock Orange)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; Aureus is grown chiefly for its bright golden spring foliage, and a little afternoon shade helps prevent scorch in hot climates.

directions: Aureus is a classic golden-foliage form of the common sweet mock orange, prized for bright chartreuse-yellow spring leaves that gradually mellow toward yellow-green through summer, offering season-long foliage color that plain-green mock orange selections lack. In late spring its arching branches carry clusters of intensely fragrant, creamy-white, four-petaled flowers with the sweet orange-blossom scent the genus is named for. Light afternoon shade helps prevent the gold foliage from scorching in hot climates while still allowing good flowering, distinguishing its site needs from the full-sun preference of most other mock orange cultivars. Plant in average, well-drained soil and prune immediately after flowering, since it blooms on old wood and later pruning removes the following year's fragrant display.

common_name: Avalanche Mock Orange (Dwarf Arching Fragrant Mock Orange)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; Avalanche has a low, wide-spreading, arching habit that stays noticeably shorter than it is wide at maturity.

directions: Avalanche is a French Lemoine-bred mock orange prized among fragrance connoisseurs as one of the most powerfully scented of all mock orange cultivars, its cup-shaped, single white flowers carrying an intense, sweet orange-blossom perfume from clusters massed along the branch tips in late spring to early summer. Unlike the larger, more upright species, Avalanche has a low, gracefully arching, wide-spreading habit that makes it noticeably shorter than it is wide at maturity, useful for a cascading effect over a low wall or bank. Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade, and prune immediately after flowering, since it blooms on old wood and later pruning sacrifices the following year's fragrant display. Established plants are easy-care and need little beyond this annual post-bloom shaping.
